newsitem.title: UK: Dixons down as profit-taking buffets sector.
newsitem.headline: Dixons down as profit-taking buffets sector.

text.p: Shares in Dixons Group Plc extended their recent loss on Thursday as some institutions reduced holdings following the stock's strong run and after recent director share sales, traders said.
Dealers said a line of stock was on offer in the market today, helping drive the share price down 11p to 521-1/2 by 1138 GMT, extending a decline since it closed at a record 577p on September 3.
Other retail stocks were also weak, with Kingfisher Plc down 9-1/2p at 638, Marks & Spencer Plc down 5-1/2p at 496 and Boots Co Plc down 3-1/2p at 632-1/2.

Standard Life, one of the UK's biggest fund managers, said in a statement it had reduced its stake in Dixons to 20.2 million shares, or 4.8 percent of the total, but gave no figure for its previous holding.
"The whole sector has had a good run and it's no wonder some of the big boys have been lightening their holdings," said one trader.
Said another, "The whole sector is showing signs of stress, it has had a good run but there is muttering about where interest rates go next and that's making people a bit nervous."
Earlier this week strategists at BZW said in a research note retail shares were showing signs of running out of steam and warned that the sector tended to peak before the peak in consumer spending.
They warned that any rise in taxes or interest rates next year could put an end to the current buoyant state of comsumer activity.

Meantime traders and analysts pointed to share sales by Dixons directors as adding to the downward pressure on the stock. Dixons said on September 24 that director Mark Souhami sold 102,620 shares after cashing in share options.
A number of other directors including chairman Sir Stanley Kalms also cashed in options earlier this month.
Analysts played down talk that the European Commission was considering new rules to increase consumer protection and allow some goods to be returned up to two years after purchase.

Such rules could undercut the appeal of the extended warranties on which Dixons makes much of its profits, but Nick Bubb, analyst at MeesPierson, said the regulations were subject to revision and were anyway five years from the statute book.
"If the rules were implemented they would cause huge problems for all retailers not just Dixons," Bubb said.
"It is a huge over-reaction, warranty scares have always been a buying opportunity and that remains the case given the company's strength of trading and the relatively undemanding rating," Bubb said.
Dixons shares have risen sharply since the beginning of 1995 and are almost three times their 190p level at the end of 1994.
